prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms confined at a magic wavelength allow many atoms to be interrogated at once and brought frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I have moved from B027 to B041. The decisive point is the scientific content of the lattice clock, which I underweighted in round 1 by reading it as metrology. Katori's magic-wavelength condition is a clean mechanism: choose the trap wavelength so that the ground and clock states see the same light shift, and the trap drops out of the transition frequency to leading order. That is exactly the kind of simple, general idea I value, and it is a different idea from the comb (2005) or from single-ion control (2012). Its consequence is concrete: thousands of atoms can be probed with Doppler and recoil effects suppressed, which is what takes statistical stability and then systematic uncertainty to 10^-18 in Ye's group and in the independent laboratories that compare such clocks. The same instrument shows many-body effects in a clock and resolves gravitational redshift over millimetres. Independent reproduction in several countries is the evidence of maturity that I asked of every other candidate, and the credit to Katori and Ye is as clean as any on the list. With five of eight round-1 files preferring it and no one arguing that it lacks maturity or clean credit, I no longer think my ranking of B041 sixth survives my own criteria.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection, which I do not dismiss, is that this is a measurement advance in a line already honoured twice, and that the fundamental-physics payoff (varying constants, dark-matter searches, redefinition of the second) is so far null or prospective. A citation that leans on the 10^-18 figure invites exactly this criticism, because that number will be superseded; the lasting content is the magic-wavelength lattice mechanism. A second reservation is attribution at the margin: Lemonde, Takamoto, Derevianko, Ludlow and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups made real contributions to the shift theory and the accuracy evaluation, and a two-name prize cannot reflect them. I also remain uneasy that my preferred pure-theory candidate is now outside my configuration, partly because the committee's opening ranking placed it nowhere else, and I cannot rule out that I am deferring to numbers; I have tried to test that by asking whether B041 stands on its science, and I think it does.

responses.point: Pearce asked whether I can show that the hexatic phase was clearly confirmed experimentally and that the 2016 citation did not cover it, and said he would then consider B027 as a possible second part alongside the clock.
responses.response: From my own knowledge, not verified against dossiers: the two-step melting scenario was tested in colloidal monolayers (Murray and Van Winkle, later Zahn, Lenke and Maret and the Konstanz group with magnetic colloids) and for hard disks by large-scale Monte Carlo (Bernard and Krauth, 2011), where the liquid-hexatic step is first order and the hexatic-solid step continuous. So the hexatic phase is real and well confirmed, but the confirmation is not uniform: the transition order depends on the interaction. That nuance is precisely what Danielsson and Eriksson have been pointing to, and it makes the universality claim weaker than I stated in round 1. On the 2016 citation, it named topological phase transitions and phases of matter, and the defect-unbinding mechanism is the intellectual core of both, so I cannot honestly claim the overlap is absent. I also agree that a second part runs into the three-person limit, since B041 already takes two names. So I do not take up your offer of a two-part prize, and I withdraw B027 as a preferred part.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice clock is both a measurement and a discovery tool, because it opens a new regime (millimetre redshift, constant tests), and that Ye appearing in other candidates is no reason to withhold the prize.
responses.response: I accept the argument. In round 1 I asked whether the committee weights metrology against discovery of a phenomenon. Your answer, that the new regime is concrete and the instrument makes new observables accessible, is convincing, and the magic-wavelength mechanism is the kind of simple idea I should reward. I would hold you to the earlier request, which I think you and Olsson share: the citation should rest on the lattice trapping at the magic wavelength and not on the record accuracy. I would also keep the null results on constant variation out of the citation, since Johansson and Lindroth rightly note they are still null.

responses.point: Danielsson holds that B004 has a clear before and after, and that the Kane-Mele theory with Molenkamp's HgTe experiment does not duplicate the 2016 prize.
responses.response: I still think the Z2 classification is a natural extension of the 2016 idea, though I accept your distinction that no magnetic field is needed, which is a real physical difference from the quantum Hall case. My main concern remains attribution: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe realisation that made Molenkamp's experiment possible, and Hasan's 3D work is also excluded, so any three-name credit is contestable. You have conceded this yourself. The chair asks whether you would move toward B041; I see B041 as having the cleaner credit, and I have moved to it for that reason, among others. I do not rank B004 among my alternatives, because I cannot defend any trio that I could not equally attack.

responses.point: Eriksson argues that the discovery in B017 is the existence of correlated insulators and superconductivity at the magic angle, not their microscopic origin, and compares this to high-Tc superconductors.
responses.response: The distinction is fair and the high-Tc comparison has force, so I no longer treat the open pairing mechanism as disqualifying on its own. I still hold two reservations. First, high-Tc was recognised after a few years of experiment on a single clear observation, but here the follow-ups by Dean, Young, Yazdani, Efetov and others are essential to what the field now regards as established, and the credit cannot carry them. Second, eight years is short and the phase diagram is still moving. I keep B017 as an alternative, and if it is brought forward I would want the citation limited to the flat-band prediction and the correlated insulating and superconducting states, with Bistritzer included as you propose.

responses.point: Johansson wants the B041 citation to name the lattice concept and its first record-level realisations so that it does not claim more than the supported contributions, and not to suggest that NIST, PTB and SYRTE did nothing.
responses.response: I agree with this and have drafted my citation in that spirit: it names the optical lattice clock and the magic-wavelength confinement and says only that frequency measurement was brought to the 10^-18 level, without asserting priority over other groups' accuracy evaluations. I would not add the fundamental-physics payoff to the citation, as you also suggest the citation lead with the clock itself. I also note your disclosure on B028 and the care you have taken; my move away from B027 is unrelated to it.

uncertainties: My recollection of hexatic experiments in colloids and of the Bernard-Krauth hard-disk result is from memory and not checked against the nomination dossiers.
Whether the committee will word the B041 citation around the magic-wavelength mechanism rather than the 10^-18 record, which will be superseded.
Whether others who contributed to lattice-clock theory and early demonstrations, such as Takamoto, Lemonde and Derevianko, can be acknowledged in the text without being credited as laureates.
Whether a theory-led statistical-physics prize such as B027 could belong to a future year if the 2016 overlap concern fades, which I cannot judge from the present discussion.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with any credited person on B041, B027 or B017. I share the Gothenburg physics environment with colleagues Johansson and Olsson at Chalmers and have no known collaboration with either, and Johansson's disclosed proximity to B028 does not affect my position on B041. I withdrew my B027 preference without any tie to its credited authors.
